thread.title: UPDATE: Fund managers just went overweight U.S. stocks for the first time in 15 months

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: Fund managers just went overweight U.S. stocks for the first time in 15 months
text:
By William Watts, MarketWatch
'Decoupling' theme draws investors away from Europe, emerging markets: survey
Global equity investors showed renewed love for U.S. stocks in June.
Bank of America Merrill Lynch said Tuesday that its June survey of global fund managers found equity investors are overweight U.S. stocks for the first time in 15 months (see chart below), with two out of three saying the U.S. has the best outlook for corporate profits--a 17-year high. The increased U.S. weighting came at the expense of emerging-market and, in particular, eurozone exposure, the survey found.
The phenomenon appears to be part of the "decoupling" story that serves as a mirror image of the synchronized global growth narrative that helped underpin equity markets in 2017. Last year, strong growth around the globe was viewed as a pillar of a world-wide stock market rally. This year, worries about growth in emerging markets and in Europe contrast with growing confidence in the U.S. economy.
Among other survey highlights, bets on large-cap tech companies, specifically the "long FAANG+BAT" position, continue to be viewed as the "most crowded" trade, topping the list for a fifth straight month. The double acronym refers to the U.S. tech giants Facebook Inc. (FB), Apple Inc. (AAPL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Netflix Inc. (NFLX) and Google parent Alphabet Inc.(GOOGL) combined with Chinese tech juggernauts Baidu Inc. (BIDU), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (BABA) and Tencent Holdings Ltd. (0700.HK).
On the bearish front, BAML analysts said a record 42% of investors believe corporations are overleveraged, which implies downside risk for equities versus government bonds.
Also, investors identified "trade war" as the biggest "tail risk" for markets, the survey found, with BAML noting that "trade tensions" have been the dominant macroeconomic worry for investors in 2018.
